We find that when a social dilemma is presented together with information about community beliefs -- but without any indication of how those beliefs should matter -- models tend to treat community belief as strategic information, so that in the Snowdrift game cooperation falls as community belief in cooperation increases. When we explicitly prompt the components of norm utility this relationship inverts, and cooperation increases with community belief, in broad agreement with the predictions of a simple norm utility model. We then show that prompting norm utility reduces the volatility of strategic decisions with respect to changes in the underlying social context, and generates more consistent reasoning habits across models. Taken together, our results suggest that prompting norm utility can help generate more human-like and consistent behavior across models and lower volatility within models.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that prompting the components of norm utility changes how three open-weight LLMs use community beliefs in one-shot social dilemmas. Without such prompting, cooperation in the Snowdrift game falls as community cooperation belief rises, and with it, cooperation rises with belief.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used both as decision aids and as models of human agents in simulation studies, so their alignment on prototypical social decisions has practical consequences, yet how they treat community beliefs is unclear.
AI.method: The authors vary community belief information in one-shot two-player social dilemmas and compare prompts that do and do not spell out norm-utility components, which are the non-material desire to conform to social norms and to be internally consistent.
AI.result: Without explicit norm-utility prompting, models treat community belief as strategic information, and cooperation falls as belief in cooperation rises. With the components prompted, the relationship inverts and broadly matches a simple norm-utility model. Prompting also reduces the volatility of decisions to changes in social context and yields more consistent reasoning across models.
AI.conclusion: Prompting norm utility may produce more human-like and consistent behaviour across models and lower within-model volatility.

title: Forgetting to Improve: Principled Data Removal in Active Learning
summary: The uncertainty of a statistical model is most commonly factorized into an aleatoric and an epistemic part. This factorization changes how predictions are interpreted in downstream decision tasks. Importantly, except for the idealistic scenario with no model mismatch, the quantification is a characteristic of the model and not the data generating process. In this paper, we propose Forgetting to Improve a method that reduces this discrepancy by incorporating the task into the modeling framework. Our key insight is to acknowledge that in scenarios of model mismatch, data can have a detrimental effect on the modeling for a specific task. Based on this insight, we propose an influence function for Gaussian process models that allows for principled removal of detrimental data samples. We showcase the flexibility of this approach by demonstrating significant improvements across a range of tasks, including Bayesian optimization, model-based reinforcement learning, and transductive learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Forgetting to Improve, which removes detrimental training samples from Gaussian process models using an influence function, so that task performance improves under model mismatch. The authors report significant gains on Bayesian optimisation, model-based reinforcement learning, and transductive learning.
AI.motivation: Under model mismatch, the aleatoric-epistemic split describes the model rather than the data-generating process, and data can harm a specific downstream task, so a model that uses all data may not be optimal for that task.
AI.method: The authors derive an influence function for Gaussian process models that identifies and removes detrimental samples in a principled way, incorporating the downstream task into the modelling framework.
AI.result: The abstract reports significant improvements across Bayesian optimisation, model-based reinforcement learning, and transductive learning but gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware removal of detrimental data is a flexible way to reduce the discrepancy between the model's uncertainty and the task's needs.

title: HybridSpec: Throughput-Aware Speculative Decoding for Hybrid GDN-MoE Models
summary: In speculative decoding, parallel drafters such as DFlash make drafting cheap, so target verification dominates each round. A central choice is the verification length, the number of tokens that the target processes in each round. Verifying more draft tokens can accept more of them, but work after the first rejection is wasted. For hybrid target models that combine Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, verification time grows much faster with this length than for dense models. In a single-request profile of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with DFlash, it grew by 71% from length 4 to 16, almost entirely in GDN and MoE layers, compared with 4%-6% for a dense Qwen3-4B target. Each GDN layer must update a recurrent state at every token and recover it at the end of the accepted prefix. The MoE cost depends on the experts that the tokens activate, which are known only once verification runs. We present HybridSpec, which selects the verification length on the GPU from draft-side acceptance estimates and measured target latency. Verification then runs this length plus one extra token up to the first MoE router, before any expert runs. There, a lightweight routing correction uses the observed expert assignments to decide whether to keep that token. The rest of verification runs only on the selected tokens. Block-parallel GDN kernels avoid storing a state after every token and reconstruct the accepted state of every GDN layer in one launch. In isolated benchmarks at verification lengths 4 to 16 with every draft token accepted, these kernels, including accepted-state reconstruction, are $1.54\times$-$4.04\times$ faster than the default kernels. With three GDN-MoE target models in single-request greedy decoding, HybridSpec is $1.75\times$-$1.88\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding and $1.30\times$-$1.33\times$ faster than DFlash.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HybridSpec, a speculative-decoding method for hybrid Gated DeltaNet and mixture-of-experts target models that picks verification length on the GPU and filters tokens at the MoE router. It is 1.75 to 1.88 times faster than autoregressive decoding and 1.30 to 1.33 times faster than DFlash.
AI.motivation: For hybrid GDN-MoE targets, verification time grows much faster with verification length than for dense models, because each GDN layer updates a recurrent state per token and MoE cost depends on experts activated only at verification time. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, verification time grew 71 percent from length 4 to 16, against 4 to 6 percent for dense Qwen3-4B.
AI.method: HybridSpec chooses the verification length from draft acceptance estimates and measured target latency. It runs the length plus one token up to the first MoE router, where a lightweight routing correction uses observed expert assignments to decide whether to keep that token. Block-parallel GDN kernels reconstruct the accepted recurrent state of each GDN layer in one launch without storing a state per token.
AI.result: In isolated benchmarks at verification lengths 4 to 16, the GDN kernels are 1.54 to 4.04 times faster than the default kernels. With three GDN-MoE target models in single-request greedy decoding, HybridSpec is 1.75 to 1.88 times faster than autoregressive decoding and 1.30 to 1.33 times faster than DFlash.
AI.conclusion: Verification-length selection and routing-aware token filtering make speculative decoding practical for hybrid GDN-MoE models, where dense-model assumptions fail.

title: Look Before You Launch: Learned Throughput Prediction for Hardware Selection in a Production Training Fleet
summary: In mixed-vendor accelerator fleets, many training jobs can run on several hardware types, and the best choice depends on each job's throughput on each type. Routing a job needs a throughput estimate for every candidate type before the job runs. We present LEAP, a machine learning performance prediction service that predicts each training job's throughput on every candidate hardware type at submission time and ranks the candidates by predicted throughput per unit cost. It routes tens of thousands of training job attempts a day across hundreds of different model types and more than 20 hardware types in a production fleet. LEAP predicts throughput from submission-time training configuration, including each job's prior throughput. LEAP reaches an accuracy of 77% over 30 nightly retrains, higher than the lookup table it replaced and at least as high as every alternative model we tested, including fine-tuned language models. Over six months, the share of eligible training GPU-hours that received a ranking by LEAP grew from 58% to 95%, and we estimate that it saves about 3% of training computational cost. In this paper, we identify the drivers that actually move accuracy and those that do not. We offer these as lessons for teams building performance predictors at fleet scale.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LEAP, a machine-learning service that predicts each training job's throughput on every candidate hardware type at submission time and ranks candidates by predicted throughput per unit cost. It routes tens of thousands of job attempts a day in a production fleet of more than 20 hardware types.
AI.motivation: In mixed-vendor accelerator fleets, the best hardware for a training job depends on its throughput on each type, which must be estimated before the job runs.
AI.method: LEAP predicts throughput from submission-time training configuration, including each job's prior throughput, and is retrained nightly. The authors compare it with the lookup table it replaced and with alternative models, including fine-tuned language models.
AI.result: LEAP reaches 77 percent accuracy over 30 nightly retrains, higher than the replaced lookup table and at least as high as every alternative tested. Over six months the share of eligible training GPU-hours that received a LEAP ranking grew from 58 to 95 percent, and the authors estimate savings of about 3 percent of training computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies which drivers do and do not move accuracy and offers these as lessons for building performance predictors at fleet scale.

title: Query-based Submodular Data Selection for Efficient Instruction Tuning
summary: As large language models are fine-tuned for increasingly specialized tasks, their performance depends more on which training examples are selected than on how many. Given a large heterogeneous training pool and a small target set specifying the desired capability, targeted data selection aims to find a compact subset that maximizes downstream performance. Existing methods score each candidate independently against the target and select the top-ranked examples, yet this point-wise strategy ignores inter-example interactions: at tight budgets the selected subset is dominated by near-redundant points that waste capacity on overlapping information. We propose Query-based Submodular functions with Gradient-guided Synthesis (QSGS), which formulates targeted selection as a submodular graph cut over a gradient similarity graph. A modular relevance term pulls selected examples toward the target task, while a pairwise dispersion penalty suppresses intra-subset redundancy. The resulting objective balances target relevance and intra-subset redundancy using the same formulation across different selection budgets. Empirically, the benefit of diversity-aware selection becomes increasingly pronounced as the data budget decreases. To further close coverage gaps that no selection from existing data can bridge, we introduce a gradient-guided synthesis step that identifies under-covered target directions via residual subspace analysis and generates synthetic examples to fill them. Experiments on MMLU, BBH, and TydiQA across Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral, show that QSGS at a 0.5% budget matches or exceeds full-data performance on Mistral-7B, outperforms the strongest baseline across all benchmarks, and yields increasing gains as the budget shrinks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes QSGS, a query-based submodular data-selection method for instruction tuning that adds gradient-guided synthesis to fill coverage gaps. At a 0.5 percent budget it matches or exceeds full-data performance on Mistral-7B across MMLU, BBH and TydiQA.
AI.motivation: Point-wise data selection ranks each candidate against the target independently and so selects near-redundant examples, which wastes capacity at tight budgets.
AI.method: QSGS formulates selection as a submodular graph cut over a gradient-similarity graph, with a modular relevance term toward the target and a pairwise dispersion penalty against intra-subset redundancy. A synthesis step finds under-covered target directions through residual subspace analysis and generates synthetic examples to fill them.
AI.result: Experiments on MMLU, BBH and TydiQA with Llama-2, Llama-3 and Mistral show that QSGS at a 0.5 percent budget matches or exceeds full-data performance on Mistral-7B and outperforms the strongest baseline on all benchmarks. Gains increase as the budget shrinks.
AI.conclusion: Diversity-aware selection matters most at small data budgets, and synthesis can cover gaps that selection from existing data cannot.

title: On the Primacy Bias in RLVR Training
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, it still remains unclear whether RLVR can extend reasoning capabilities beyond what is already encoded in the base model. In this paper, we study this question through the lens of primacy bias: the tendency of models to over-rely on already-learned representations, disproportionately improving performance on problems they already handle well while underexploring harder ones that require departing from those representations. Through our controlled experiments and large-scale analysis, we show that RLVR training on mixed data tends to further sharpen performance on easier problems while yielding only marginal gains on harder ones. We find that although hard problems lead to modest gains overall, they are actually the ones that help most in expanding the model's reasoning capabilities and pushing the representations. However, prolonged training on these hard problems may also hurt and lead to forgetting on easy problems. These findings help to better understand some of the prior conflicting observations about RLVR, specifically, why on (OOD) domains where the base model performs poorly, improvements on hard problems can expand reasoning; while on well-trained domains, forgetting can reduce performance and mask genuine gains obtained from hard problems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies RLVR training and finds that mixed-data training mainly sharpens performance on easy problems, while hard problems give modest average gains but help most in expanding reasoning. Prolonged training on hard problems can cause forgetting on easy ones.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) extends reasoning beyond what the base model already encodes, and prior results on this seem to conflict.
AI.method: Through the lens of primacy bias, the tendency of models to over-rely on learned representations, the authors run controlled experiments and large-scale analysis of RLVR on mixed-difficulty data.
AI.result: RLVR on mixed data sharpens easy problems and gives only marginal gains on hard ones. Hard problems help most in expanding reasoning and reshaping representations, but prolonged training on them can hurt easy-problem performance through forgetting.
AI.conclusion: The conflicting prior results can be explained by domain coverage: on out-of-distribution domains where the base model is weak, hard-problem gains can expand reasoning, while on well-trained domains forgetting can mask those gains.

title: AlgoPilot: Cross-Paradigm Reasoning in Language Models via Strategy Selection and Guidance
summary: Real-world problems span diverse domains, including program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization, and often require fundamentally different solution paradigms. A central challenge for LLM-based reasoning is twofold: identifying an appropriate problem-solving approach and formulating it correctly. In this paper, we propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that enables adaptive selection of the solving approaches and structured problem formulation prior to execution. The AlgoPilot framework contains three components: 1) a SteerLM, trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), that adaptively selects the solving strategy (paradigm and modes) based on input problems, 2) the corresponding expert GuideLM, trained via SFT, that generates structured formulation guidance tailored to the selected strategy, and 3) an ExecutionLM that generates solutions conditioned on both the selected strategy and its formulation. Unlike prompting-based methods that rely on fixed reasoning templates, our approach learns to adaptively choose and structure problem-solving strategies based on the input. We build AlgoPilot on Qwen3-8B and evaluate across 5 problem categories and 13 benchmarks with 66 unique domains, comparing against both the latest similarly scaled small models and large LLMs. AlgoPilot significantly improves average accuracy for the same model from 38.4% to 72.9%, outperforming the best large LLM prompting baseline GLM-5 by 11.7%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component. Notably, we show that the learned steering and formulation modules can transfer across execution models, suggesting their potential to improve other LLMs. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that learns to select a solving strategy, generate formulation guidance for it, and execute the solution. Built on Qwen3-8B, it raises average accuracy across 13 benchmarks from 38.4 to 72.9 percent and outperforms GLM-5 prompting by 11.7 percent.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning needs both the right solving paradigm and a correct formulation of the problem, and prompting methods that use fixed reasoning templates do not adapt the strategy to the input.
AI.method: AlgoPilot has three components: SteerLM, trained with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, that selects the paradigm and modes; GuideLM, trained with supervised fine-tuning, that writes formulation guidance for the selected strategy; and ExecutionLM, which generates solutions conditioned on both.
AI.result: Average accuracy for the same model rises from 38.4 to 72.9 percent across 5 problem categories and 13 benchmarks with 66 unique domains, outperforming the best large-LLM prompting baseline, GLM-5, by 11.7 percent. Ablations confirm each component, and the learned steering and formulation modules transfer across execution models.
AI.conclusion: Learned strategy selection and formulation can transfer across execution models and may improve other LLMs.

title: The Agent Board: Kanban for Machines; Durable Coordination for Agents That Outlive the Conversation
summary: Harnesses for large language models have converged on a single-threaded shape: one agent, one history, one machine, one sitting. That shape fails work that spans many agents, outlives any one model call, or waits on systems that are not agents. We describe the Agent Board, the coordination substrate in the Corvic harness. The board is a durable, shared table of semi-semantic tasks: a few exact fields the system routes on, and a free-form body that only language models read. Agents post tasks, watch tasks, and block on them, ending their turn and holding no process until a matching post wakes them. A system agent, the Board Keeper, acts as the interrupt handler for the board: it carries events from non-agent parts of the harness onto the board, matches them to waiting tasks by reading their prose, and allocates new agents for tasks that name a kind of agent rather than an instance. Loadable coordination policy kernels give statuses and roles meaning for a given pattern of work, without the board enforcing them. The design mirrors the kanban board a human team puts on a wall. We argue it is what persistent agent products such as Meta Muse, OpenAI dots and SpaceXAI Grok Bot need once an agent must wait, hand off work, or work with agents from another vendor. We view the board as an operating-system scheduler for agents and state where the analogy breaks. We separate what the mechanism guarantees from what it leaves to convention, and report a trace from a live board and three small simulated pilots. In the pilots, the wait cost of the board was flat in wait length while naive polling grew about 165-fold, but a plain external watcher was cheaper than the board. The Board Keeper matched prose waiters with no false wakes but missed 3.6 percent of real wakes.

AI.tldr: The paper describes the Agent Board, a durable shared task table in the Corvic harness for coordinating agents that outlive a single conversation or wait on non-agent systems. In three simulated pilots, board wait cost stayed flat as wait length grew while naive polling grew about 165 times, but a plain external watcher was cheaper.
AI.motivation: Single-threaded harnesses with one agent, one history, and one machine fail for work that spans many agents, outlasts model calls, or waits on non-agent systems.
AI.method: The board holds semi-semantic tasks, with a few exact routing fields and a free-form body read only by language models. A system agent, the Board Keeper, carries events from non-agent parts of the harness onto the board, matches them to waiting tasks by reading their prose, and allocates agents for tasks that name a kind of agent. Loadable coordination policy kernels give statuses and roles meaning without the board enforcing them.
AI.result: In three small simulated pilots and a trace from a live board, board wait cost was flat in wait length while naive polling grew about 165-fold, but a plain external watcher was cheaper than the board. The Board Keeper produced no false wakes and missed 3.6 percent of real wakes.
AI.conclusion: The board is useful as a durable coordination substrate, with the analogy to an operating-system scheduler breaking in places the authors identify, though it is not cheaper than a simple watcher in these pilots.

title: Structured Clinical Memory as Context for Probabilistic Decision Models: A Synthetic Evaluation with Jev
summary: Longitudinal clinical context is often distributed across noisy, repetitive forms and narrative records. We study whether a compact structured memory can improve a probabilistic decision model's answers when the underlying patient vignette is already available. We created 30 fully synthetic cases spanning twelve clinical domains, paired each with synthetically generated structured memory, and evaluated 120 typed questions with Jev. The raw-vignette arm achieved 90.0% accuracy (95% normal-approximation confidence interval: 84.6%-95.4%); adding memory achieved 93.3% (88.9%-97.8%). Five questions changed from incorrect to correct and one changed in the opposite direction (exact McNemar $p=0.219$). Choice log loss decreased from 0.258 to 0.175 and binary Brier score from 0.054 to 0.022. Memory added 310 input tokens per call on average, while observed mean latency was unchanged at approximately 0.5 seconds. These results are directionally positive rather than clinically validating: the cases are synthetic, the labels are single-author judgments, and the memory is an oracle upper bound rather than extracted production output. The pilot supports evaluating structured clinical memory as a reusable state interface for decision models.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether a compact structured clinical memory improves a probabilistic decision model's answers on 30 synthetic cases and 120 typed questions. Adding memory raised accuracy from 90.0 to 93.3 percent, and the result is described as directionally positive rather than clinically validating.
AI.motivation: Longitudinal clinical context is spread across noisy forms and narrative records, and a compact structured memory might help a decision model when the patient vignette is already available.
AI.method: The authors created 30 fully synthetic cases across twelve clinical domains, paired each with synthetic structured memory, and evaluated 120 typed questions with the Jev decision model in a raw-vignette arm and a memory arm. The memory is an oracle upper bound rather than extracted output.
AI.result: The raw-vignette arm reached 90.0 percent accuracy (95 percent CI 84.6 to 95.4) and the memory arm 93.3 percent (88.9 to 97.8). Five questions became correct and one became incorrect (exact McNemar p = 0.219). Choice log loss fell from 0.258 to 0.175 and binary Brier score from 0.054 to 0.022. Memory added 310 input tokens per call with unchanged mean latency of about 0.5 seconds.
AI.conclusion: The pilot supports evaluating structured clinical memory as a reusable state interface for decision models, but the synthetic cases, single-author labels, and oracle memory limit the claims.

title: The Evolution Strategies Paradox: Better Models from Worse Perturbations
summary: How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.

AI.tldr: The paper characterises the Evolution Strategies (ES) paradox, in which all offspring of a parent model perform worse than the parent while the parent keeps improving during ES fine-tuning of LLMs. It explains the paradox through the local reward landscape and the properties of the ES estimator.
AI.motivation: Perturbation-based methods such as ES can optimise billion-parameter LLMs, yet classical search depends on finding good candidates in each population, so the paradox needs explanation.
AI.method: The authors characterise the phenomenon across models, tasks, and modalities, then examine how the local reward landscape and the ES gradient estimator contribute to it.
AI.result: In high-dimensional spaces, individual exploratory perturbations perform worse but still point in good directions, and aggregating those directions yields local improvements. The abstract reports the paradox recurs across models, tasks, and modalities, but gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The paradox is a byproduct of a principled interaction between noise and curvature, and it offers guidance for perturbation-based fine-tuning and for high-dimensional optimisation in general.

title: GlucoAgent: Personalized Glucose Forecasting from Multimodal Personal Context
summary: Continuous glucose monitors, smartwatches, meal logs, and health profiles form a rich multimodal personal context that can significantly enhance glucose forecasting. However, existing methods struggle to effectively utilize these signals to improve glucose prediction because the relevance of different modalities varies drastically across individuals and time. We present GlucoAgent, an LLM-based agentic system that addresses this challenge through dynamic, case-by-case analysis at inference time. For each forecast, GlucoAgent writes and runs code over an individual's multimodal context and returns predictions with a reason and supporting evidence. The generated programs are highly diverse, ranging from retrieving similar past meals to fitting and back-testing physiological and statistical models. On CGMacros, a multimodal glucose dataset, GlucoAgent outperforms time series foundation models on every forecasting horizon, achieving an average RMSE of 22.5 mg/dL compared to 23.5 mg/dL of Chronos-2, the leading multimodal time series foundation model. Furthermore, GlucoAgent is highly effective at leveraging multimodal data. The addition of multimodal data reduces its average RMSE by 1.4 mg/dL (24.0 mg/dL to 22.5 mg/dL), compared to a marginal 0.3 mg/dL (23.8 mg/dL to 23.5 mg/dL) improvement for Chronos-2. This advantage is most pronounced in challenging post-meal windows, where GlucoAgent uses multimodal context to reduce 60-minute forecast RMSE by 4.6 mg/dL (31.0 mg/dL to 26.5 mg/dL), far exceeding the 0.8 mg/dL (31.9 mg/dL to 31.1 mg/dL) reduction achieved by Chronos-2.

AI.tldr: The paper presents GlucoAgent, an LLM-based agent that writes and runs code over a person's multimodal context to forecast glucose at inference time. On CGMacros it achieves an average RMSE of 22.5 mg/dL against 23.5 for Chronos-2, and its post-meal 60-minute RMSE falls from 31.0 to 26.5 mg/dL.
AI.motivation: Continuous glucose monitors, smartwatches, meal logs and health profiles can improve forecasting, but the relevance of each modality varies across individuals and over time, which existing methods handle poorly.
AI.method: For each forecast, GlucoAgent writes and runs code over the individual's multimodal context and returns predictions with a reason and supporting evidence. The generated programs range from retrieving similar past meals to fitting and back-testing physiological and statistical models.
AI.result: On CGMacros, GlucoAgent outperforms time-series foundation models at every horizon, with an average RMSE of 22.5 mg/dL against 23.5 for Chronos-2. Adding multimodal data lowers its RMSE from 24.0 to 22.5 mg/dL, against 23.8 to 23.5 for Chronos-2. In post-meal windows, 60-minute RMSE falls from 31.0 to 26.5 mg/dL for GlucoAgent, against 31.9 to 31.1 for Chronos-2.
AI.conclusion: Case-by-case agentic analysis makes better use of multimodal personal data than foundation models do, and the advantage is largest in post-meal windows.

title: Interpretable Early Termination of Web Navigation Agents via Closed Sequential Pattern Mining
comment: In online proceedings of AI Agents for Discovery in the Wild (AID-Wild) Workshop at ACM CAIS 2026
summary: Web navigation agents built on open-weight language models fail often and fail late, with most of the tokens spent after the trajectory has become unrecoverable. Recent work has shown that early termination is a viable cost-reduction strategy, but existing approaches produce opaque termination decisions that do not support diagnosis or human oversight. In this work we apply closed sequential pattern mining (BIDE+) to K-step prefixes of agent execution traces to produce a small, human-reviewable failure-signature library that organizes into a four-category failure taxonomy with associated repair recommendations. We use a multi-variant evaluation protocol that explicitly removes contamination artifacts (zero-step crashes and trivially separable single-step successes) so that reported detection accuracy reflects behavioral discrimination rather than trace-length distributions. We evaluate our methodology on 1,544 MiniWoB++ traces collected from three open-weight language models, achieving the best F1 at K=3 on the Exclude-errors configuration across eight methods (0.717), recovering 88% of test-set failures within three steps, and supporting an early-termination policy that saves 26.3% of tokens at 92% precision.

AI.tldr: The paper applies closed sequential pattern mining (BIDE+) to early prefixes of web-agent traces to build an interpretable failure-signature library that supports early termination. On 1,544 MiniWoB++ traces it reaches F1 0.717 at K=3 and saves 26.3 percent of tokens at 92 percent precision.
AI.motivation: Web-navigation agents on open-weight models fail often and late, with most tokens spent after the trajectory has become unrecoverable, and existing early-termination methods give opaque decisions that do not support diagnosis or human oversight.
AI.method: The authors mine closed sequential patterns from K-step prefixes of execution traces to form a small, human-reviewable failure-signature library organised into a four-category failure taxonomy with repair recommendations. They use a multi-variant protocol that removes zero-step crashes and trivially separable single-step successes.
AI.result: On 1,544 MiniWoB++ traces from three open-weight models, the best F1 at K=3 under the Exclude-errors configuration is 0.717 among eight methods. The method recovers 88 percent of test-set failures within three steps and an early-termination policy saves 26.3 percent of tokens at 92 percent precision.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable pattern mining can support early termination of web agents with diagnostic value, at a modest accuracy level.

title: Palimpsestic Accountability in the US Federal AI Inventories
summary: An AI inventory is a structured, often public record in which a government or organization lists and describes the AI systems it uses or plans to use. Studies of single AI inventory releases describe what systems do but say little about how they are governed over time. We linked entries across three releases of the US Federal AI Use Case Inventory (2023--2025), compared answers only where both releases required them, and analyzed governance accounts through a dual deductive-inductive approach, guided by the Algorithmic Decision-Making Adapted for the Public Sector (ADMAPS) framework. As the inventory grew from 710 to 3,611 entries from 2023 to 2025, fewer required answers were left blank, but accountability was rewritten through three mechanisms. Each release \emph{redrew} the scope of the questions; agency-assigned classifications \emph{gated} what was reported; and answers were also \emph{overwritten}, with gains and losses concentrated in single agencies and little account of human oversight and judgment. These findings show that each release redraws the boundary of accountability and leaves the public to \emph{re-stitch} the records, a condition we term \textbf{palimpsestic accountability}. We recommend versioned records, reasons for every reclassification, public files that distinguish kinds of missing answers, and oversight documented as conditions to improve public sector AI accountability.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses three releases of the US Federal AI Use Case Inventory (2023 to 2025) and finds that accountability is rewritten across releases through redrawn questions, agency-gated classifications, and overwritten answers. The authors call this palimpsestic accountability.
AI.motivation: Studies of single AI inventory releases describe what systems do but not how their governance changes over time, which matters for public-sector accountability.
AI.method: The authors link entries across the three releases, compare only answers that both releases required, and analyse governance accounts with a dual deductive-inductive approach guided by the ADMAPS framework.
AI.result: The inventory grew from 710 to 3,611 entries, and fewer required answers were left blank. Accountability changed through three mechanisms: each release redrew the scope of questions, agency-assigned classifications gated what was reported, and answers were overwritten, with gains and losses concentrated in single agencies and little account of human oversight.
AI.conclusion: Each release redraws the boundary of accountability and leaves the public to re-stitch the records, and the authors recommend versioned records, reasons for reclassification, distinct kinds of missing answers, and documented oversight.

title: Validation-Gated ML Pipeline Synthesis with Expert-Grounded Self-Evolving Skills
summary: Recent advances in large language models have enabled agentic systems that automate machine learning pipeline construction from minimal user input. However, existing agentic AutoML methods either depend on rigid templates that limit adaptability, target narrow task domains, or rely on free-form code generation that lacks reliability guarantees, leaving intermediate errors to propagate silently and degrade the final model. We present EvoML, an agentic framework for end-to-end ML pipeline synthesis built on expert-grounded skills that evolve across runs, executed through a validation-gated harness. The framework decomposes pipeline construction into four phases coordinated by three agents: an Orchestrator that enforces validation gates, advancing each phase only when its outputs pass structural, execution, and semantic checks, which precludes error propagation and keeps every artifact auditable; an Executor that runs expert-grounded skills, grounded in the nnU-Net workflow and pairing reusable templates with online adaptation; and a Curator that performs post-run evolution, consolidating the scripts and guidance recovered during a run into the skill library so it improves across datasets. We evaluate EvoML on eight datasets spanning six sophisticated, real-world ML task types, against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools. EvoML achieves full automation and the best final model quality on all eight, spanning segmentation (up to 0.94 Dice), classification (0.99 accuracy), reconstruction (0.95 SSIM), and denoising (0.79 normalized PSNR), while transferring to broader ML tasks.

AI.tldr: EvoML is an agentic framework that synthesizes end-to-end ML pipelines from expert-grounded skills that evolve across runs and are executed through validation gates. It reports full automation and the best final model quality on all eight evaluated datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic AutoML methods rely on rigid templates, target narrow task domains, or use free-form code generation without reliability guarantees, so intermediate errors propagate silently and degrade the final model.
AI.method: Three agents coordinate four pipeline phases: an Orchestrator enforces validation gates (structural, execution and semantic checks) before each phase advances, an Executor runs expert-grounded skills grounded in the nnU-Net workflow with reusable templates and online adaptation, and a Curator consolidates the scripts and guidance recovered during a run into a growing skill library.
AI.result: On eight datasets spanning six real-world ML task types, EvoML achieves full automation and the best final model quality on all eight against agentic AutoML systems and command-line coding tools, with up to 0.94 Dice for segmentation, 0.99 accuracy for classification, 0.95 SSIM for reconstruction and 0.79 normalized PSNR for denoising.
AI.conclusion: Validation-gated, self-evolving skills make ML pipeline synthesis more reliable and auditable, and the approach transfers to broader ML tasks.

title: Clocks all the way down: does sequence-processing AI need endogenous temporal structure?
summary: Mainstream sequence-processing AI is temporally reactive: each update is driven by input and learned state transitions, rather than by an independently evolving internal temporal reference. Biological brains, by contrast, continuously generate rhythmic activity that structures perception, memory, and cognition, and this rhythmicity reaches all the way to behavior. We ask whether this difference is merely implementational or genuinely computational. Four lines of evidence suggest that endogenous temporal structure supports putative functions that input-driven architectures may not readily replicate: 1) phase-dependent routing of information, 2) delay-structured combinatorial representation, 3) cross-frequency multiplexing of items, and 4) oscillation-gated offline consolidation. A proof-of-concept delay-ablation test dissociates representational capacity from memory retrieval. In recurrent and spatial spiking networks with fixed synaptic weights and connectivity, shuffling delays preserves part of the capacity but substantially impairs the sequence retrieval. The relative contrast is more pronounced for spatial networks and longer propagations. Instantaneous transmission collapses capacity itself. We then outline a cross-frequency multiplexing scheme that combines item identity and serial order with alternative mechanisms for selective memory retrieval. Finally, we state one falsifiable hypothesis, conditions for matched-resource tests, and three research directions: the components already exist; the disciplined comparison does not.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper asks whether the lack of an endogenous, independently evolving temporal reference in sequence-processing AI is computationally significant. A delay-ablation test in fixed spiking networks shows that shuffling delays impairs sequence retrieval more than it reduces representational capacity.
AI.motivation: Mainstream sequence-processing AI is driven by input and learned state transitions, whereas biological brains generate rhythmic activity that structures perception, memory and behavior; it is unclear whether this difference is merely implementational or genuinely computational.
AI.method: The paper reviews four lines of evidence (phase-dependent routing, delay-structured combinatorial representation, cross-frequency multiplexing and oscillation-gated offline consolidation), runs a delay-ablation test in recurrent and spatial spiking networks with fixed synaptic weights and connectivity, and outlines a cross-frequency multiplexing scheme together with one falsifiable hypothesis.
AI.result: Shuffling delays preserves part of the capacity but substantially impairs sequence retrieval, with a more pronounced contrast for spatial networks and longer propagations; instantaneous transmission collapses capacity itself.
AI.conclusion: Endogenous temporal structure plausibly supports functions that input-driven architectures may not readily replicate, and the authors call for disciplined matched-resource comparisons, which they note have not yet been done.

title: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation
summary: Frontier LLM agents can turn known vulnerabilities into working exploits, but are costly and often access-restricted due to their potential for malicious use. Open-weight models offer a more accessible alternative, but struggle to maintain progress across long exploitation chains. They also often fail to apply relevant security knowledge at the appropriate stage and in the right context to identify and evaluate promising attack directions. To address these limitations, we propose DoGNAVY-Exploit, a multi-agent harness built around two complementary designs: stage-aware decomposition with progressive expert knowledge disclosure, and hierarchical orchestration with parallel exploration. Specifically, DoGNAVY-Exploit uses configurable milestones to recast long-horizon exploitation as short, verifiable capability transitions and provides only the knowledge relevant to each stage. Within each milestone, a hierarchical architecture separates strategic planning from parallel execution: a planner proposes diverse attack routes, executors test them concurrently, and a controller accepts progress only when supported by runtime evidence. A shared structured memory consolidates verified facts, artifacts, replay steps, and failed routes across branches, allowing agents to build on collective progress and carry validated knowledge into subsequent milestones. In controlled benchmark environments, DoGNAVY-Exploit with GLM-5.2 achieves 97.5% Pass@1 on Cybench, and 97.5% zero-day and 100% one-day Pass@1 on CVE-Bench. On ExploitGym, it solves 79 tasks with GLM-5.2 and 157 with GLM-5.3, while the corresponding public Claude Code baselines solve 39 and 130 tasks, respectively. Ablation results further demonstrate that the stage-aware orchestration, expert knowledge, parallel exploration, and memory designs can substantially improve the exploitation capabilities of open-weight agents.

AI.tldr: DoGNAVY-Exploit is a multi-agent harness that lets open-weight models carry out long-horizon vulnerability exploitation in controlled benchmarks, reaching 97.5% Pass@1 on Cybench and 97.5% zero-day and 100% one-day Pass@1 on CVE-Bench with GLM-5.2.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLM agents can turn known vulnerabilities into exploits but are costly and access-restricted, while open-weight models struggle to sustain progress across long exploitation chains and to apply security knowledge at the right stage.
AI.method: Long-horizon exploitation is recast as configurable milestones with stage-specific expert knowledge; within each milestone a planner proposes diverse attack routes, parallel executors test them, and a controller accepts progress only with runtime evidence, while a shared structured memory keeps verified facts, artifacts, replay steps and failed routes across branches.
AI.result: With GLM-5.2 it solves 79 ExploitGym tasks versus 39 for the public Claude Code baseline, and with GLM-5.3 it solves 157 versus 130; ablations indicate that stage-aware orchestration, expert knowledge, parallel exploration and memory each substantially improve exploitation capability.
AI.conclusion: Structured multi-agent scaffolding can substantially improve the exploitation capability of open-weight agents, as shown in controlled benchmark environments.

title: Toward User-Centered Agentic Recommendation: When Does Platform Competition Benefit Users?
summary: Conventional recommender systems operate within platform-specific catalogs, limiting access to potentially valuable resources across platforms. We propose user-centered agentic recommendation, a paradigm in which user agents compare recommendations from competing platform agents, and formalize their interaction as a repeated game. Platforms strategically modify descriptions without changing intrinsic item value, while each user agent assesses platform credibility using feedback from consumed items only. Our analysis shows that expanded resource access need not improve user welfare: strategic misrepresentation and limited verification can offset the benefits of platform competition. We quantify when platform credibility assessment allows users to benefit from broader access despite strategic exaggeration. Our analysis identifies resource and reporting conditions that guarantee higher average welfare than the original platform with an interaction budget linear in platform count. Experiments on synthetic and Amazon-grounded markets show that credibility assessment can improve finite-horizon utility, while its benefits depend on market size and mechanism parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes user-centered agentic recommendation as a repeated game between user agents and competing platform agents and shows that broader resource access does not necessarily improve user welfare, because strategic misrepresentation can offset the gains.
AI.motivation: Conventional recommender systems are confined to platform-specific catalogs, and it is unclear whether letting user agents compare recommendations across competing platforms benefits users when platforms can strategically exaggerate item descriptions.
AI.method: Platforms modify descriptions without changing intrinsic item value, and each user agent assesses platform credibility using feedback from consumed items only; the interaction is analyzed as a repeated game and tested on synthetic and Amazon-grounded markets.
AI.result: The analysis identifies resource and reporting conditions that guarantee higher average welfare than the original platform with an interaction budget linear in the number of platforms; experiments show that credibility assessment can improve finite-horizon utility, with benefits depending on market size and mechanism parameters.
AI.conclusion: Platform competition benefits users only under specific conditions, and credibility assessment can counter strategic exaggeration, so the gains from broader access are not automatic.

title: DualWorldBench: Can Agents Plan Deliveries across Symbolic and Grounded Worlds?
summary: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website this https URL.

AI.tldr: DualWorldBench is a benchmark for testing whether agents can plan multi-goal pickup-delivery tasks across symbolic and grounded worlds, and it finds that agents struggle to turn local understanding into globally consistent plans.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of multimodal agents use simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, so it is unclear whether agents can integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical and multimodal constraints.
AI.method: The benchmark is built on a shared pickup-delivery interface with three components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding and planning.
AI.result: In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences; perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning.
AI.conclusion: The central challenge is composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans, and the benchmark, with its datasets and code publicly available, serves as a testbed for tighter perception-reasoning-planning integration.

title: Exact Optimality Certification of QPLIB 2096 through Complete Set Partitioning
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables including one appendix table. Jingyang Du and Zixiong Yi contributed equally to this work and share first authorship. Corresponding author: Yang Shen
summary: We present an exact computational proof that the frozen QPLIB_2096 instance has global minimum 7,025,720. The solution and certification approach was explored and refined through ZiYor, a self-evolving AI system. The authors provide the mathematical account and exact validation reported here. The original formulation has 300 binary variables, 6,900 triangle inequalities, and 25 nonconvex quadratic constraints. A coefficient-level reconstruction identifies its variables with the unordered pairs of 25 items. The triangle inequalities encode partitions, while each quadratic constraint becomes a bound on the total weight of edges incident to one partition block. This yields a set-partitioning formulation over all capacity-feasible blocks, with a separate edge-cost graph determining the objective. Exact enumeration examines 245,505 subsets of sizes one through six and finds 14,981 feasible blocks. Every six-element subset is infeasible; nonnegative capacity weights exclude all larger blocks. An integer price vector satisfies the dual inequality for every feasible block and has sum 2,229,456. Subtracting this sum from the total objective edge cost 9,255,176 gives a lower bound of 7,025,720, attained by the supplied six-block partition. Fresh solver-free checks validate the candidate against both frozen model formats and verify the certificate. The result is an instance-specific optimality proof with an exact primal and dual witness; no cross-instance performance conclusion is drawn.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an exact computational proof that the QPLIB_2096 instance has global minimum 7,025,720, with an explicit primal partition and a dual certificate. The solution was explored and refined with the ZiYor self-evolving AI system.
AI.motivation: The instance is a nonconvex quadratic binary problem with 300 binary variables, 6,900 triangle inequalities and 25 nonconvex quadratic constraints, and the paper seeks an exact, checkable optimality certificate for it.
AI.method: A coefficient-level reconstruction identifies the variables with unordered pairs of 25 items; the triangle inequalities encode partitions, and each quadratic constraint bounds the total weight of edges incident to one block, giving a set-partitioning formulation over capacity-feasible blocks with a separate edge-cost graph for the objective.
AI.result: Exact enumeration of 245,505 subsets finds 14,981 feasible blocks and shows that every six-element subset is infeasible; an integer price vector with sum 2,229,456 satisfies the dual inequality for every feasible block, and subtracting it from the total edge cost 9,255,176 gives a lower bound of 7,025,720, attained by the supplied six-block partition.
AI.conclusion: This is an instance-specific optimality proof with exact primal and dual witnesses, validated by solver-free checks; the authors draw no conclusion about cross-instance solver performance.

title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds
summary: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

AI.tldr: AceAction is a dataset of human keyboard-and-mouse gameplay across multiple 3D games, annotated with hierarchical goals (overall instructions, ordered subgoals and local skill instructions) for training vision-language-action agents.
AI.motivation: Existing game-based VLA datasets are limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not reflect changes in task objectives, and collecting such data in physical environments is costly.
AI.method: Demonstrations are organized around complete tasks and linked to temporally aligned visual observations and actions; a vision-language-model pipeline identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions.
AI.result: The demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries; an audit of 500 trajectories gives a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments.
AI.conclusion: The dataset provides a foundation for studying how agents execute, combine and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

title: Neologism Inoculation Prompting
summary: Inoculation prompting is a method to reduce undesired behaviours such as reward hacking in frontier models. It works by training a model on harmful examples under a prompt that specifies the undesired behaviour, which reduces the model's tendency to exhibit it unless prompted. However, the inoculation prompt is written in plain English, so any user can re-elicit the behaviour easily. We introduce neologism inoculation prompting (NIP), which replaces the English prompt with a new token that is trained on the frozen model and removed at deployment. NIP outperforms other inoculation methods, and performs competitively with gradient routing despite being simpler. It also works on reward hacking, but fails on sycophancy and harassment. Using control tokens and analyses of activations, we identify the mechanism for this as NIP hiding the harmful behaviour behind an unreachable region of model inputs, rather than deleting it. More broadly, our work suggests that neologisms can be a powerful way to carve out and shape access to behaviours that are undesired or harmful.

AI.tldr: Neologism inoculation prompting (NIP) replaces the plain-English inoculation prompt with a new token trained on the frozen model and removed at deployment. It outperforms other inoculation methods at reducing reward hacking but fails on sycophancy and harassment.
AI.motivation: Inoculation prompting reduces undesired behaviors such as reward hacking, but its plain-English prompt can be used by any user to re-elicit the behavior.
AI.method: NIP trains a model on harmful examples under a newly introduced token, trained on the frozen model, instead of an English prompt, and removes the token at deployment; control tokens and activation analyses are used to study the mechanism.
AI.result: NIP outperforms other inoculation methods and performs competitively with gradient routing despite being simpler; it works on reward hacking but fails on sycophancy and harassment; the analyses suggest it hides the harmful behavior behind an unreachable region of model inputs rather than deleting it.
AI.conclusion: Neologisms can be a powerful way to carve out and shape access to undesired or harmful behaviors, though the approach does not work equally across behavior types.

title: Reliability Stress Testing of RAG Retrieval under Query-Relevant Corpus Poisoning
summary: External text can affect a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system only after the retriever admits it to the model context. We stress this admission step while varying document content, attacker query information, per-target poison budget, and contamination scope. Across 623 Benchmarking Information Retrieval (BEIR) queries from SciFact and NFCorpus, five query-targeted documents per query reduce classical-retriever nDCG@10 by 40.2-61.5% in isolated-target stress. Full-query anchoring explains most Best Matching 25 (BM25) degradation, whereas appended text also shifts latent semantic analysis (LSA) and Hybrid rankings. A pretrained BGE-small validation reaches 100% target exposure for query-only P=5 on both datasets; adding the injection payload changes SciFact nDCG only from 0.269 to 0.271 and lowers NFCorpus exposure slightly to 98.8%, indicating that query anchoring remains the dominant retrieval-side factor for this dense model. Query length materially changes the interpretation of partial-information attacks: on 162 long SciFact queries, two random terms cover 19.9% of eligible terms and still yield 39.5% Hybrid target exposure. Multi-target contamination adds cross-target interference. Overlap-based admission can remove full-query poisons but may sharply reduce clean retrieval utility, and maximal marginal relevance (MMR) leaves exposure unchanged under the tested configuration. The study measures retrieval-layer failures, not downstream instruction following.

AI.tldr: The paper stress-tests the retrieval step of RAG under query-relevant corpus poisoning and finds that five query-targeted documents per query reduce classical-retriever nDCG@10 by 40.2-61.5%, with query anchoring as the dominant retrieval-side factor.
AI.motivation: External text can affect a RAG system only after the retriever admits it into the model context, so the robustness of this admission step to query-targeted corpus poisoning needs direct measurement.
AI.method: Across 623 BEIR queries from SciFact and NFCorpus, query-targeted documents are injected while document content, attacker query information, per-target poison budget and contamination scope are varied; BM25, LSA and Hybrid retrievers, a pretrained BGE-small validation, overlap-based admission and maximal marginal relevance (MMR) are examined.
AI.result: Five query-targeted documents per query reduce classical-retriever nDCG@10 by 40.2-61.5% in isolated-target stress; BGE-small reaches 100% target exposure for query-only poisoning with P=5 on both datasets, and the injection payload changes SciFact nDCG only from 0.269 to 0.271; on 162 long SciFact queries, two random terms still yield 39.5% Hybrid target exposure; overlap-based admission can remove full-query poisons but may sharply reduce clean utility, and MMR leaves exposure unchanged in the tested configuration.
AI.conclusion: Query anchoring is the dominant retrieval-side factor for this dense model, and the study measures retrieval-layer failures only, not downstream instruction following.

title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
comment: Code: this https URL Keywords: Language model agents, agent harnesses, reinforcement learning, harness complementarity, harness routing
summary: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

AI.tldr: Harness-S trains a single policy to absorb repairs from sibling harnesses: when all attempts under the base harness fail, rollouts under auxiliary harnesses replace the failed group in reinforcement learning, and the trained policy outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness.
AI.motivation: Harness variants repair different failures and their utility changes as the policy learns, so there is no universally superior harness to search for, and failures of a base execution system need to be rescued selectively.
AI.method: Directional Harness Evolution builds a fixed Sibling Harness Pool of specialized harnesses along distinct repair directions; Complementary Harness Rescue Training uses this pool only when all base attempts fail; an Adaptive Harness Router selects Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs, with policy-aware profile re-anchoring as the policy learns.
AI.result: Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness; behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy, and reusing the router for Rank-1 inference gives additional gains at the same executor rollout count.
AI.conclusion: Capabilities elicited by auxiliary harnesses can be transferred into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness without the auxiliary harnesses at deployment.

title: Bidirectional Centered Score Matching for Discrete Diffusion Distillation
summary: Discrete diffusion models with parallel decoding are often distilled using token-wise KL objectives. Although token-wise KL exactly matches the corresponding product-form block distributions, its probability-space optimization geometry and teacher-only candidate truncation may provide insufficient supervision under aggressive few-step distillation. Concrete Score Matching (CSM) provides an alternative within-position objective by aligning relative logit geometry, but its complete pairwise form incurs $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|^2)$ complexity. We propose Bidirectional Centered Score Matching (BCSM), an efficient within-position distillation objective that constructs an $\mathcal{O}(K)$ bidirectional active set, reduces pairwise comparisons to $\mathcal{O}(K^2)$, and factorizes them into an $\mathcal{O}(K)$ objective. We further introduce cross-timestep transition alignment. Experiments demonstrate strong quality--efficiency trade-offs, including up to $6\times$ NFE reduction with a 16.9\% relative HumanEval gain and a 15.1\% relative MMMU gain at single-step inference.

AI.tldr: Bidirectional Centered Score Matching (BCSM) is an efficient within-position distillation objective for discrete diffusion models that aligns relative logit geometry over an O(K) bidirectional active set, with up to 6x NFE reduction and 16.9% relative HumanEval and 15.1% relative MMMU gains at single-step inference.
AI.motivation: Token-wise KL distillation of parallel-decoding discrete diffusion models may give insufficient supervision under aggressive few-step distillation because of its probability-space geometry and teacher-only candidate truncation, while complete pairwise Concrete Score Matching costs O(|V|^2).
AI.method: BCSM constructs an O(K) bidirectional active set, reduces pairwise comparisons to O(K^2) and factorizes them into an O(K) objective, and further introduces cross-timestep transition alignment.
AI.result: Experiments show strong quality-efficiency trade-offs, including up to 6x NFE reduction, a 16.9% relative HumanEval gain and a 15.1% relative MMMU gain at single-step inference.
AI.conclusion: A within-position score-matching objective can be made linear in the active-set size K while improving few-step distillation of discrete diffusion models.

title: OSGR: Observation-Support Graph Reasoning for Earth Observation Question Answering
summary: Answering geographic queries over Earth observation (EO) archives requires solving a joint retrieval-and-derivation problem under strict spatiotemporal constraints. Existing LLM agents fail to ground observation items or suffer from search-space explosion. We propose OSGR, a two-stage framework that factorizes this search into offline symbolic concept deduction and online Relation-Conditioned Grounding. OSGR leverages an offline Observation-Support Graph to deduce valid target-to-result support paths at the concept level, and applies spatiotemporal compatibility kernels to instantiate grounded observation-item sets. On Earth-Bench and DisasterM3-Reason, OSGR improves GPT-4o accuracy from 49.3\% to 63.7\% while reducing the execution-step ratio from 2.9 to 2.5.

AI.tldr: OSGR is a two-stage framework for geographic question answering over Earth observation archives that separates offline symbolic concept deduction from online grounding, raising GPT-4o accuracy from 49.3% to 63.7% on Earth-Bench and DisasterM3-Reason.
AI.motivation: Answering geographic queries over Earth observation archives requires joint retrieval and derivation under strict spatiotemporal constraints, and existing LLM agents either fail to ground observation items or suffer search-space explosion.
AI.method: An offline Observation-Support Graph deduces valid target-to-result support paths at the concept level, and online Relation-Conditioned Grounding applies spatiotemporal compatibility kernels to instantiate grounded observation-item sets.
AI.result: On Earth-Bench and DisasterM3-Reason, OSGR improves GPT-4o accuracy from 49.3% to 63.7% while reducing the execution-step ratio from 2.9 to 2.5.
AI.conclusion: Factorizing the search into offline concept deduction and online grounding improves accuracy and reduces execution steps for Earth observation question answering.

title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI
comment: Accepted at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r = 0.72-0.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated. ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role, and state subspaces and steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable. Across long-horizon memory, state maintenance, tool use, least-privilege coordination, and embodied stress tests, ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines. Against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; against MemoryArena-Agent it gains up to 4.8 points. It gains 10.7-12.1 points under perturbation, reaches 93.5% role consistency, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2). Ablating the joint task-role-state span costs 7.2 points against 0.8 for a matched-rank random span, indicating these directions are functionally implicated, not incidental; supplying them by prompt or retrieval recovers 4.3 points less. ATLAS is therefore a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents.

AI.tldr: ATLAS is a training-free intervention that steers agent hidden states toward a shared subspace encoding the active task, assigned role and current shared state, reducing task drift, role drift and state staleness in long-horizon open-weight multi-agent systems.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from task drift, role drift and state staleness, which existing methods address separately at the surface-text level or by treating control directions independently; a pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns suggests the three share a representational cause.
AI.method: ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role and state subspaces and acts on hidden states before each token is generated, steering them toward shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable.
AI.result: ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory and activation-steering baselines across stress tests; against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; it reaches 93.5% role consistency, gains 10.7-12.1 points under perturbation, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2); ablating the joint task-role-state span costs 7.2 points versus 0.8 for a matched-rank random span.
AI.conclusion: ATLAS is a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents, and the directions it uses are functionally implicated rather than incidental.

title: Planning-Coding Separation in LLM-Based Code Generation: An Empirical Study
summary: Planning has been identified as an important factor for improved code generation with Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the interaction between planning capability and coding capability remains largely underexplored, especially when the two capabilities are from different LLMs. In this paper, we conduct the first comprehensive empirical study of planning-coding interaction in LLM-based code generation, where planning and coding are assigned to different LLMs (i.e., planning-coding separation). Specifically, we explore different planner-coder combinations to investigate the effectiveness for coders to utilize planning information from various planners and the impact of further training of coders on planner-coder combinations. Our results demonstrate that almost all planner-coder combinations are as competitive as using the same LLM for planning and coding, and the combination of a stronger planner and a stronger coder typically achieves improved effectiveness. Furthermore, using a large model as the planner paired with a much smaller model as the coder can sometimes be as competitive as using the large model as both the planner and the coder, and further training of the coder can typically boost various planner-coder combinations. These findings provide empirical evidence that planning and coding can be separated to a considerable extent in LLM-based code generation, which may offer a more flexible way to construct code-generation systems.

AI.tldr: An empirical study finds that separating planning and coding across different LLMs is almost always about as competitive as using one LLM for both roles, and that a large planner paired with a much smaller coder can match a large model doing both jobs.
AI.motivation: Planning improves LLM-based code generation, but how planning capability interacts with coding capability when the two come from different LLMs has been largely underexplored.
AI.method: The authors evaluate many planner-coder combinations, measuring how effectively coders use planning information from various planners and how further training of the coder affects these combinations.
AI.result: Almost all planner-coder combinations are as competitive as using the same LLM for planning and coding; a stronger planner with a stronger coder typically performs better; a large planner with a much smaller coder can sometimes match the large model in both roles; further training of the coder typically boosts various combinations.
AI.conclusion: Planning and coding can be separated to a considerable extent, which may allow more flexible construction of code-generation systems.

title: ATC: Agent Trajectory Control for Role-Contract Enforcement in Black-Box Multi-Agent Systems
comment: Accepted at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems assign different responsibilities to different agents: one plans, another retrieves evidence, another verifies, another executes. This division of labor is only meaningful if each agent stays within the functions it is authorized to perform. Over many turns, however, an agent can produce a locally reasonable message that exercises authority belonging to another role: a verifier that begins planning, a retriever that asserts unsupported conclusions, an executor that changes state no one approved. We formalize this as role drift, a turn-level breach of an agent's role contract. We introduce Agent Trajectory Control (ATC), which makes each role's authority explicit as a contract and enforces it at the point where a message would enter the shared conversation. ATC scores a proposed output for out-of-role deviation, leakage into the functions of other roles, impermissible speech acts, and logical contract breaches, then computes a leakage-regularized target that constrains regeneration; the revised message is re-checked before admission. Enforcement acts on the message rather than the generator, so ATC governs agents whose internal representations are unavailable. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous teams, ATC improves task performance and role consistency while lowering role-drift energy relative to strong baselines spanning prompting, memory, workflow control, and activation editing, with the largest gains under explicit role-confusion stress tests and in larger, more diverse teams.

AI.tldr: ATC makes each agent's role authority an explicit contract and enforces it on every message before it enters a shared multi-agent conversation, improving task performance and role consistency while lowering role drift in black-box teams.
